definition: A hypothetical AI that would surpass human intelligence across virtually all domains.
details: A hypothetical AI that would surpass human intelligence across virtually all domains. ASI is central to long-term AI-safety discussions about alignment and control.

explainer.lead: Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, is a hypothetical AI whose thinking would far exceed human ability in nearly every area that matters. It is not a system that exists today, but the possibility shapes research into AI safety, alignment, control, and governance because such a system could be extremely difficult to manage.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a student who could learn almost every subject better than the best human teachers, then keep improving their own way of learning. That is the idea behind ASI: a computer mind far smarter than people across almost all tasks. People discuss it now so they can think about safety and rules before anything like it might exist.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers encounter ASI primarily as a future scenario in safety, alignment, control, and governance work, not as a capability available in current tools. A common design scenario is recursive self-improvement, where an AI improves its own intelligence and becomes better at making further improvements, potentially producing an intelligence explosion. Forecasts are highly uncertain, so neither a near-term product roadmap nor the abilities of an existing model establish that ASI is imminent.
tiers.paperLevel: Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence defines superintelligence as "any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest". One proposed route is recursive self-improvement: an AI improves itself, becomes more capable of further improvement, and potentially triggers an intelligence explosion; machine speed, modularity, and coordination offer additional possible advantages. ASI remains hypothetical, surveyed researchers have little consensus on when human-rival machine intelligence may arrive, and the extent and timing of existential risk are disputed.

explainer.example: Imagine a human-level AI that can design a slightly better version of its own reasoning system. That version designs a better successor, and each cycle becomes faster and more effective; repeated enough times, this recursive self-improvement could produce an intelligence explosion and an ASI that reasons millions of times faster than people.

usedIn.name: AI safety and alignment research
usedIn.detail: ASI frames long-term questions about keeping a vastly more capable system aligned with human intentions and under meaningful control.

usedIn.name: AI governance and policy
usedIn.detail: Proposals include international treaties to prevent superintelligence from emerging and recommendations for governing its development.

usedIn.name: Technology forecasting
usedIn.detail: Researchers use scenarios and surveys to explore possible routes to ASI and the large uncertainty around when advanced machine intelligence might appear.

explainer.intuition: Human-level AI would match people broadly; ASI would go much further, outperforming even the most gifted humans across virtually all domains. The key idea is not simply knowing more facts, but having overwhelmingly greater general cognitive performance.
howItWorks: An AI first reaches roughly human-level general intelligence.
It extends those abilities beyond human performance.
If it can improve itself, each improvement may make further improvements easier.
Rapid hardware, larger computational capacity, or coordinated systems could amplify its capabilities.
The result would dominate humans across arbitrary tasks, though this remains a hypothetical scenario.
explainer.whyItMatters: A system with such broad superiority could be hard to predict, align, or control, which is why ASI is central to discussions of existential risk. It also prompts present-day debate over governance, development restrictions, and whether safety research should take priority.
misconceptions: ASI is not another name for today's chatbots or other existing AI systems.
Artificial general intelligence means broad human-level ability, while ASI greatly exceeds humans in virtually all domains.
There is no agreed timetable for ASI, and expert forecasts vary widely.
Recursive self-improvement is a proposed route, not a demonstrated path to ASI.
